about: The Prologue of Saint John, read at the end of Mass at the Gospel side. The priest signs with the cross first the altar or the book, then himself — forehead, lips and breast — as before any Gospel, and reads the fourteen verses that carry the whole story back behind the making of the world. At the words “Et Verbum caro factum est” he genuflects. The hand missal prints those five words in capitals and carries the rubric besides; do and the typical edition set a rubric — all mean the same thing. The announcement has its answer, “Glória tibi, Dómine”, and the whole closes with “Deo grátias”.

s01.narrative: Then the priest goes to the Gospel side, joins his hands, and says:

s04.narrative: And signing with the sign of the cross first the altar or the book, then himself on the forehead, the lips and the breast, the priest says:

s05.translation: The beginning of the holy Gospel according to John.

s07.narrative: With his hands joined the priest continues:

s08.translation: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by Him, and without Him was made nothing that was made: in Him was life, and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

s09.translation: There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. This man came for a witness, to bear witness of the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but was to bear witness of the light.

s10.translation: It was the true light, which enlightens every man that comes into this world. It was in the world, and the world was made by Him, and the world knew Him not. He came unto His own, and His own received Him not. But as many as received Him, to them He gave power to become sons of God — to them that believe in His name: who are born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

s12.translation: And the Word was made flesh,

s14.translation: and dwelt among us; and we saw His glory, the glory as of the Only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.

w007.function: Nominative: this is a heading, not a sentence — the priest announces what he is about to read.

w008.function: Agrees with “Evangélii” (w009); evangélium is neuter, hence sancti and not sanctæ.

w012.function: A sentence with no verb: Latin does not supply “be”.

w015.function: The same words open the book of Genesis in the Latin Bible — In princípio. John begins his Gospel at the beginning of everything.

w018.function: Neuter, and so is everything that agrees with it. Latin Verbum renders the Greek Lógos.

w022.function: Apud with the accusative means at someone's side, in someone's presence — company, not means.

w025.function: Two nominatives in one sentence: “Deus” and “Verbum” (w027). Which is the subject is not settled by form — Latin has no articles — but by the run of sentences, which is about the Word.

w028.function: Neuter, because it points back to the Word.

w034.function: Neuter plural: literally all things. English keeps the plural, and the verb with it.

w037.function: With “sunt” (w038) it forms the perfect passive: facta sunt — “were made”.

w044.function: The subject of the sentence, though the word is indeclinable: the corpus states the case, number and gender the sentence gives it — the form itself marks none.

w045.function: Both editions attach the relative clause “quod factum est” to what precedes rather than to what follows: both set a comma before quod and a colon after est. That pointing is the whole of the decision — the ancients read the sentence both ways.

w056.function: Genitive plural: the light belonging to men, given to men.

w060.function: The noun has only a plural — in Latin darkness is always “darknesses”.

w061.function: A present tense among past ones: it shone and shines still.

w064.function: Feminine, because “lux” (w058) is a feminine noun in Latin.

w066.function: The verb means both to seize and to grasp with the mind, and the sentence does not force a choice: the darkness neither laid hold of the light nor understood it.

w069.function: A passive participle in the nominative, agreeing with “homo” (w068).

w072.function: Dative of possession: “to whom the name was John”, that is, whose name was John.

w077.function: Perfect, not present: the form is the same for both, but the narrative runs in the past — “Fuit” (w067), “erat” (w074).

w082.function: Imperfect subjunctive in a purpose clause after “ut” (w080) — past, because the main clause is past.

w086.function: An adjective used as a noun: the masculine plural means all men.

w093.function: A predicate nominative: with “esse” Latin puts the predicate in the same case as the subject.

w107.function: Accusative, so it agrees with “hóminem” (w106) and not with the light: it is the man who comes into the world. The Greek allows both readings; the Latin form does not.

w126.function: An adjective with no noun, neuter plural: “the things that were his own” — his home, his inheritance, his country.

w129.function: A different word from “própria” (w126) — suus is the reflexive possessive — in the same substantival use, now masculine: there his own things, here his own people.

w140.function: Accusative with the infinitive “fíeri” (w142): Latin puts the complement in the accusative because the whole phrase depends on “potestátem” (w139).

w143.function: Dative plural, in apposition to “eis” (w138): it picks them up again so that the relative clause can be attached — to them, that is, who believe.

w145.function: A present among perfects: the believing goes on, while the rest of the sentence tells what happened.

w152.function: A plural where English has a singular — a Hebraism: “of bloods” means simply “by ordinary begetting”.

w164.function: A deponent participle: passive in form, active in meaning. With “sunt” (w165) it forms the perfect — they were born.

w168.function: A predicate nominative, and feminine — yet the participle “factum” (w169) is neuter, because it agrees with the subject, the Word, and not with the flesh.

w176.function: First person plural — the one first-person verb in this reading: we saw.

w180.function: It does not equate but compares: glory such as befits the Only-begotten.

w181.function: An adjective used as a noun, in the genitive: the glory belonging to the Only-begotten.

w184.function: Neuter, and this sentence has no neuter noun in it: “glóriam” (w179) is feminine and “Unigéniti” (w181) genitive. The only word the form can agree with is “Verbum” (w167), a whole sentence back. The corpus claims the nominative on that ground and marks the case disputed.
